The Lean implementation defines OFE equivalence (≡) on BI propositions as definitionally equal to bi-entailment (⊣⊢): Equiv P Q := P ⊣⊢ Q. The Rocq implementation takes a different approach: ≡ comes from the OFE structure, ⊣⊢ is defined separately, and bi_mixin_equiv_entails connects the two.

  1. I think both enforce the same constraint, but what was the rationale for defining Equiv P Q := P ⊣⊢ Q rather than following Rocq's approach?

I'm porting big_ops, but the Rocq proofs extensively use generalized rewriting which is currently missing in Lean.

  1. Was the rw' tactic intended to support ⊣⊢ rewriting? If so, what's the path forward — extend rw' or a different approach?
  2. In the meantime, what's the recommended approach for porting proofs that rely on generalized rewriting?

1: I'm not sure why exactly it is like this but it is equivalent.
2: There was some discussion of this in Lars König's original development which we have moved to proofmode.md. rw' is pretty limited. If you search in this channel there was some experiments with supporting generalized rewriting (search the Zulip for various attempts). You're free to pick this up if you want.
3: Generalized rewriting just searches for appropriate NonExpansive lemmas to apply around the your rewrite. We have been doing this by hand, and so far it has not been too hard. How bad is it in big_ops?
To rewrite R under a nonexpansive function f the pattern is generally something like refine .trans (f_ne.ne R) ?_). Generalized rewriting just automates the search for f_ne.ne.

I'm far from an expert on this matter, but I thought I'd mention that mathlib has had a generalised rewriting tactic grw for a while now, see here for the implementation and documentation.

Unlike Rocq's generalised rewriting, grw (as with rw) doesn't support rewriting under binders. I'm not sure how big of a limitation this is as I'm not an expert here. I also wonder if Iris could benefit from using this instead of rw', though I imagine this tactic (along with its dependencies) would need to be moved out of mathlib for that.

What's the status quo on this? For now I see that there are a lot of proofs in Iris Lean which almost look like Agda in how they use no tactics, but explicit .trans calls. Is the plan to support grw at some point?

Term mode is generally preferred as it is more readable and more stable. There are no plans to support grw for proofs inside Iris, but at the user-facing level, we might look into something similar at some point.

Another problem is that grw is part of Mathlib and Iris Lean does not (and should not) depend on Mathlib. So grw could only be supported for users as part of a Iris-Lean-Mathlib package (which is planned to exist at some point).
5 messages were moved from this topic to #iris-lean > Mathlib dependence by Shreyas Srinivas.

Markus de Medeiros said:

Term mode is generally preferred as it is more readable and more stable.

That doesn't match my experience in Rocq at all. But maybe the tradeoff is different in Lean.

This indeed also is opposite of my experience in Rocq, but the Lean editing experience makes a huge difference here. In particular, the fact that you can place your cursor at any point in a term and see the context and goal state at that point changes the tradeoff quite a bit. It still took me some time to get used to the term mode in Lean, but now I think it is quite nice.
(And Claude is surprisingly good at writing term mode proofs. When porting, I often leave holes for the proof terms and ask Claude code to fill them. I would say it works roughly 80% of the time, especially if you also copy the Rocq proof in the file such that it can look at it.)

Actually, speaking of rewriting, since we work in Lean, why don't we just change the OFE definition to have equiv_dist : x = y ↔ ∀ n, Dist n x y and drop Equiv? I just did it, and reached COFE solver (albeit I skipped some constructions that are not related to guarded types) with zero sorry's.
That would allow us to reuse existing rewrite infra.

We can discuss it tomorrow, but my argument in favor of that is:

  • Lean automation relies on classical axioms and funext/propext, so trying to be axiom-free is not pragmatic, since any simp or grind can introduce it. Already some theorems use LEM/funext/propext.
  • IMO, one of the key points of porting Iris to Lean is to have access to mathlib, which does not avoid the axioms above.
  • Trying to avoid in Rocq makes sense, because in this case one doesn't restrict to a particular class of models. I'm not sure if it is possible in Lean, but since axioms are part of Init, it seems that only classical models are considered.
  • That would be easier than quotienting OFE's by equivalence (i think we discussed it at some point).
  • That would be a massive UX improvement (both for maintainers and users).

Personally, I would really appreciate it, since I was planning to port GItrees at some point, and having access to usual rewrite would save countless problems of working with it without generalized rewrite tactics.

I guess, one point that we should be careful about is whether the new equiv_dist holds for all constructions that are in Iris.
It definitely works for CCC structure on OFE's, SProp, and for the guarded types, but I haven't checked it for other provided algebras. Does anyone know examples for which it could fail?
This would require quotients to define an OFE with non-trivial equivalence
It's the same as saying all OFE's are Leibniz (in our current definition), which yes could in principle be forced to be made true using quotient types.

Do you remember some examples with non-trivial equivalences? From the top of my head, it seems that agree is one example, where we would need to quotient lists by permutation modulo distance, but I might be wrong and there're more.
If most of the examples are simple, then, perhaps, it is worth discussing this change. The ability to use rewrite tactic would be nice to have.

I'm not confident that it would be a good idea even if most OFEs are simple. We can chat tomorrow of course, but this would be a fundamental divergence from Iris and would make keeping Iris-Lean up to date more uncertain.

Some better options might be to see if we can wrap rewrite in some metaprogramming for OFE's that are actually Leibniz, or to see if Mathlib's grw tactic can work for our purposes and either copy/paste it or put it in Iris-Lean-Math (yet to be created). I also experimented with getting grind to solve OFE rewriting problems (general setoids actually) and it kind of worked but needed a really fragile grind extension. Could be a potential solution for your use case though too!
Our Std/Rewrite.lean also has the rewriting tactic from the initial iris-lean thesis, it's been long enough that I forget what it was missing but you can look for that too

I think we should seriously explore this proposal by @Sergei Stepanenko. As Sergei says, this would give quite big benefits since a lot of Leans infrastructure is based on = and it would unlock powerful tactics like simp and grind. The main question for me is whether this would actually work for all OFEs that we care about. In particular, this would also imply that bi-entailment in the separation logic corresponds to equality, which would be very powerful. But I am not sure if it actually holds. In particular, can we prove that equiv on UPred co-incides with equality? It is not obvious to me that this holds because of the ✓{n} x →:

structure UPred (M : Type _) [UCMRA M] where
  holds : Nat → M → Prop
  mono {n1 n2 x1 x2} : holds n1 x1 → x1 ≼{n2} x2 → n2 ≤ n1 → holds n2 x2

instance : OFE (UPred M) where
  Equiv P Q := ∀ n x, ✓{n} x → (P n x ↔ Q n x)

Michael Sammler said:

In particular, can we prove that equiv on UPred co-incides with equality? It is not obvious to me that this holds because of the ✓{n} x →:

I don't understand the issue. UPred itself would also need to become a quotient, so it would hold by construction, no? Or am I not understanding something?
The question is whether you can prove this property without making UPred a quotient, but by keeping the current definition. It seems like it almost works except for the ✓{n} x →.

I see, I thought we were more broadly considering adapting the current definitions to follow more closely how they appear in the "Iris from the ground up" paper. There, they describe OFEs such that

It follows that, as nnn increases, =n\overset{n}{=}=n becomes more and more refined (OFE-MONO). In the limit, it agrees with plain equality (OFE-LIMIT).

And UPred is also directly defined as a quotient over ≡\equiv≡. I wouldn't be surprised if taking one step requires the other, but I'm not certain either.

Michael Sammler said:

In particular, can we prove that equiv on UPred co-incides with equality? It is not obvious to me that this holds because of the ✓{n} x →:

That's a fair point. I haven't considered UPred, and it looks like for UPred we will need quotients. That's the part that might be hard to do, as logical connectives will need to be redefined by quotient lifting. In principle, it should work, as all logical connectives in Rocq Iris have proper instances wrt bi-entailment.

I think you could probably make it work by defining UPred as follows:

structure UPred (M : Type _) [UCMRA M] where
  holds : (n : Nat) → {x : M // ✓{n} x} → Prop
  mono {n1 n2 x1 x2} : holds n1 x1 → x1.1 ≼{n2} x2.1 → n2 ≤ n1 → holds n2 x2

For this, you get

example (P Q : UPred M) : (∀ n x, ✓{n} x.1 → (P n x ↔ Q n x)) → P = Q := by intro _; ext; grind

(One probably wants to wrap {x : M // ✓{n} x} into a nice definition.)

Ha. I was just partway through writing something similar. An alternative is to make a class TrivialValid for trivially valid CMRA's, and then UPred M for TrivialValid M is Leibniz.

Just to put it out there, you do regular Lean rewriting using Leibniz OFE's, you just have to do rw [eq_of_eqv H] instead of rw [H].

To continue being a cynic (I agree this would be nice but I am just skeptical that it would work) this OFE definition is also untrue for the standard library maps which aren't extensional. You could force everyone to use extensional maps but that means no maps in nested inductive types.

Michael Sammler said:

I think you could probably make it work by defining UPred as follows:

structure UPred (M : Type _) [UCMRA M] where
  holds : (n : Nat) → {x : M // ✓{n} x} → Prop
  mono {n1 n2 x1 x2} : holds n1 x1 → x1.1 ≼{n2} x2.1 → n2 ≤ n1 → holds n2 x2

For this, you get

example (P Q : UPred M) : (∀ n x, ✓{n} x.1 → (P n x ↔ Q n x)) → P = Q := by intro _; ext; grind

(One probably wants to wrap {x : M // ✓{n} x} into a nice definition.)

That's a nice solution! And it would help to avoid redefining most of logical connectives.
We can put it for the meeting agenda tomorrow, and if we agree that it is worth pursuing, I can try to setup a branch with this experiment to see if it works well. There are a lot of details that would be interesting to investigate.

Markus de Medeiros said:

Just to put it out there, you do regular Lean rewriting using Leibniz OFE's, you just have to do rw [eq_of_eqv H] instead of rw [H].

That is a fair point, but to me it seems like it probably doesn't work with IProps, all cameras should be Leibniz (so no ElemG, only fully provided GFunctor) and there would be a non-trivial threading of it through the recursive domain equation solver.
For my use case with GItrees it would probably work, but also only if all ground types are fixed in advance and Leibniz.

Markus de Medeiros said:

To continue being a cynic (I agree this would be nice but I am just skeptical that it would work) this OFE definition is also untrue for the standard library maps which aren't extensional. You could force everyone to use extensional maps but that means no maps in nested inductive types.

Also a fair point! That would force the extensionality for maps. I am not sure what are the consequences for users.

In any case, we should probably discuss some solution to rewriting (either that, or copying grw, or something else), because while currently it makes sense to write bi-entailments and equivalences by hand, it might become a problem if someone wants to build something bigger on top of the port.

Sergei Stepanenko said:

That is a fair point, but to me it seems like it probably doesn't work with IProps, all cameras should be Leibniz (so no ElemG, only fully provided GFunctor) and there would be a non-trivial threading of it through the recursive domain equation solver.

You're totally right. In that case it makes quite a lot of sense to internalize validity for UPred like Michael suggested!
yeah the actual CMRA you instantiate Iris with is basically never TriviallyValid or Leibniz

Markus de Medeiros said:

To continue being a cynic (I agree this would be nice but I am just skeptical that it would work) this OFE definition is also untrue for the standard library maps which aren't extensional. You could force everyone to use extensional maps but that means no maps in nested inductive types.

I think it is great that you are a cynic about this and using this to point out potential problems with this! This is a lot better than discovering a lot later after a lot of work. So please keep it up :)
The point about non-extensional maps is a good one. I am not fully sure about the implications of it though. Maybe one cast an non-extensional map to an extensional map before putting it into an OFE?

even if you make ≡ the same as =, you still have to deal with rewriting for dist n, right? that cannot be resolved using quotients. is that so much rarer that it's still worth it? in many cases in rocq we have the same lemmas for ≡ and dist n and the proof is basically copy-pasted, so removing just one of those proofs would not save that much work.

Sergei Stepanenko said:

And it would help to avoid redefining most of logical connectives.

dont you still have to redefine them? everywhere that hold is being invoked you now have to prove validity

ralfj said:

even if you make ≡ the same as =, you still have to deal with rewriting for dist n, right? that cannot be resolved using quotients. is that so much rarer that it's still worth it?

This is indeed one concern I share with this approach. However, in my experience rewriting with ≡ is a lot more common than rewriting with dist n, especially as a user of Iris that wants to rewrite with bi-entailment. Actually, with this approach I am more concerned about rewriting with entailment |- than rewriting with dist n. Rewriting with entailment appears relatively often (not sure if more or less often than bientailment) and this approach would not provide a solution for this. Allowing rewriting with bientailment would probably still be a significant win though.

ralfj said:

dont you still have to redefine them? everywhere that hold is being invoked you now have to prove validity

Sure, but that proof seems like it should be quite trivial. For most definitions (e.g. /\, \/, ∃, ∀, ...) you can just thread the proof through. For wand one gets the validity proof as an assumption and for star you use that validity distributes over op. The definition of entailment also already contains the validity proof.

Michael Sammler said:

a user of Iris that wants to rewrite with bi-entailment.

that's not very common among users, is it? the proofmode mostly replaces it.
but it is quite common in the core BI theory that cant yet use the proofmode, so maybe that makes it worth it. (or maybe iris-lean could set things up a bit differently so that the proofmode can be used earlier.)

... actually as you say that's mostly rewriting with entailment, not bi-entailment.

I’m a bit cautious about this change. The benefits aren’t very clear to me. As discussed and based on my experience, Bi-entailment rewriting isn’t very commonly used by users nor in BI theory. Entailment rewriting seems to be the pain point. I’m not sure how this change will address it. Markus mentioned it would make Iris-lean to diverge from Iris-Rocq, potentially complicating the porting and future synchronisation. IMO, this may outweigh the potential gain. We should discuss and evaluate this aspect.

I just had a look at the grw implementation in mathlib here and it does not seem to be too dependent on mathlib. Maybe one could upstream it into batteries? Does anyone have experience with upstreaming things from mathlib to batteries?
No experience but I asked about it (before the job got punted down my priority queue) #batteries > Requesting to move stuff from Mathlib into Batteries?

For completeness, here is my the grind extension for setoid solving I generated a while ago. It has not been human-reviewed aside from checking that the proofs succeed, but it did kind of work. I read that there were eventually going to be plans to add setoid rewrites to grind for real, but I didn't see a timeline.
Wondering: would Agree become Leibniz (provided its argument type is Leibniz) if we used a (multi?)set instead of a list?

the reasoning would be non-trivial but I think it holds (classically)... for every element in A you'd end up with an infinite sequence of elements in B that are closer and closer (dist n-related for higher and higher n). assuming the sets are finite that implies the existence of a single element in B that is equal to A at all n, and then using Leibniz of the element type you get that it is =-equal.
does Lean have extensional finite sets with arbitrary element types?
Nice! This might be a good change try at some point. Yes the Lean standard library has such sets.

To share an example of an OFE which is not Leibniz, for good reasons. One thing I'm thinking about is real random variables as resources (ie. where ownership implies knowledge of a lower bound, for example). You want to work with resources with almost-sure equality but not equality itself: 

noncomputable section
open Iris ProbabilityTheory MeasureTheory
variable {Ω : Type _} [MeasurableSpace Ω]

@[ext] structure RandomVariable (δ : Type _) (μ : Measure Ω) where
  car : Ω → δ

namespace RealRandomVariableMax
variable {μ : Measure Ω}
/-- OFE for ae equality of the random variables -/
scoped instance aeOFE : OFE (RandomVariable ℝ μ) where
  Equiv x y := x.car =ᵐ[μ] y.car
  Dist _ x y := x.car =ᵐ[μ] y.car
  dist_eqv := {
    refl _ := ae_eq_rfl
    symm := (Filter.EventuallyEq.symm ·)
    trans := (ae_eq_trans · ·)
  }
  equiv_dist := .symm <| forall_const _
  dist_lt H _ := H

Just so it doesn't get lost, here's a branch where I did a small experiment with it: https://github.com/Kaptch/iris-lean/tree/eq-test

I changed only OFE and COFESolver, and it is messy 10 minute sketch, but the COFESolver works, and gets propositional equality for folding and unfolding.

Also, probably it's not a big gain for most of the use cases. As was discussed, for UPred you can get the same result for free (currently, I'm experimenting with it, and will make a PR, if it works well).
After thinking about it, changing OFE's would probably mostly benefits projects that make use of other recursive domain equations, which are not propositions (e.g., GItrees or potentially some other domain theory applications).

Hi all,

A small update on the discussion we had before.

  1. The modification to UPred that Michael suggested, works with no issues. The modification is relatively simple, and requires only minor updates to UPred constructors. And since it is possible to show that UPred is Leibniz, we can use it for rewriting by showing bi-entailment. If it is interesting for people, we possibly can discuss it. Of course, it will help for rewriting only along bi-entailment, but in comparison to grw, it would allow to rewrite under binders, which might help with reasoning about bigOps.
  2. For other recursive domain equations, it is possible instead to push Leibniz through the recursive domain equation solver. As it practice these equations rarely include non-Leibniz OFEs, it should suffice for most of the cases. E.g., here's an equation for lambda calculus that gives propositional equality for folding and unfolding.

If one (or both) of these points above sound reasonable to integrate, I can make a few passes over it, and make a PR.
The first change requires modification to UPred, and the second one just adds some minor additional lemmas.
Both of these look very impressive! I think they're probably good to have in Iris-Lean.

Update on both proposals:

  • New UPred is here. Since that's a change to one of the core definitions, probably it's better to ask around if it might break something for projects using Iris. I've talked with Amin, and he couldn't remember any extra UPred constructors or modalities that might break with this definition, but it's still better to be careful than careless.
  • Leibniz preserving functors are here. It doesn't change any core functionality, and simply adds some instances for common functor shapes, but it's probably useful only for a handful of Iris projects that rely on setoid rewriting for guarded types, such as Actris or GITrees.

I'm not sure if those should be merged, since it's a mild divergence from the Rocq implementation, and probably until we reach a consensus on rewriting, they can be pending.

I'm in favour of merging after review! Super cool stuff. We should flag it with an -- EXPERIMENT comment with a link to this Zulip thread by the new definition of UPred (that's what we did for the definition of OFunctors, which you can see we also changed from Rocq).

regarding UPred, personally I'm not worried about the difference to Rocq. This is a case where eningeering tradeoffs differ between the two systems (in Rocq, even this adjusted definition would not be leibniz due to a lack of proof irrelevance). there are already much bigger differences e.g. in the handling of quantifiers in the BI interface.
Also, ~nobody actually interacts with the internals of UPred.
Thanks for your comments! Okay, then I will add the link, and make a few more passes before merging.

I feel like we're getting close to genuinely needing generalized rewriting. My experience is that without generalized rewriting Lean proofs can be up to 4x longer and quite unreadable; and porting proofs is very much not a tactic-by-tactic translation.
I guess now we try out Mathlib's generalized rewriting in IrisMath (unless you think writing our own is better)
Trying out the Mathlib one is a good idea!
I also recently met @Jovan Gerbscheid who worked on this. I will ask what he thinks effort-wise about moving grw to batteries.

For instance https://github.com/suhr/iris-lean/blob/cc795893825c280d15e193db84908481d69f2dec/Iris/Iris/Instances/Lib/GhostMap.lean#L202, and other long proofs in the same file.

For instance https://github.com/suhr/iris-lean/blob/cc795893825c280d15e193db84908481d69f2dec/Iris/Iris/Instances/Lib/GhostMap.lean#L202, and other long proofs in the same file.

Ah, yeah. I did a pass over it (now that there was finally no file contention haha) and while a lot of the maps stuff was cuttable/refactorable, some of the proofs are still uglier than the Rocq versions.

As far as it goes, my checklist to support building proofs in core Iris based on grw would be

  • No mathlib dependency
  • Stable, or clear how to debug when it fails (Our proofs are already kind of a setoid hell, I'd prefer not to redo them every 4 weeks)
  • Compatible with the typeclass-based approach (I'm a little worried given that regular rw sometimes needs a lot of information to figure out what our types are, but there might be a way around this)

Now that I hear there's a path to the first bullet being possible, it would definitely be worthwhile to experiment with bullets 2 and 3 in IrisMath
